Decreased thickness of the summer trout habitat in Lake Jocassee is at least partially due to the operation of the Jocassee Pumped Storage facility and the Oconee Nuclear Power Project located on Lake Keowee. The Oconee Nuclear Project uses Lake Keowee as a source of condenser cooling water, thereby causing some warming of Lake Keowee. The Jocassee Pumped Storage units withdraw water from Lake Jocassee during generation and draw water from Lake Keowee during pumping. Applicant has presented an analysis of the impact of the Jocassee units on Lake Jocassee trout habitat, stating that plant operation is presently exerting the maximum impact that would be expected from this source. However, Staff analysis of the available data indicates that there is potential for greater impact on trout habitat in Lake Jocassee in the future from Jocassee station operation as well as from operation of the proposed Bad Creek station. These impacts are discussed in Section 3.2.2.3.
2.2.3 Unique and Other Biotic Resources
2.2.3.1 Flora
The Highlands Biological Station, Inc., conducted a survey of the gorges in the general vicinity of the Bad Creek Project for the purpose of recommending certain locations for protective natural areas due to their biotic uniqueness (Bruce, 1974). In the proposed project area, two locations were recommended: the west fork of Howard Creek, and a ridge between Bad Creek and West Bad Creek supporting a stand of Fothergilla major, a rare shrub. In the northeast facing cove of the west fork of Howard Creek, a good example of cove vegetation exists. Many of the species here are commonly found in the north, and are at the extreme of their southern range. The Highlands Biological Station recommends preservation of these two areas or, at least, relocation of some Fothergilla plants. The Applicant has transplanted 26 Forthergilla specimens out of the project area.
The Applicant sponsored a botanical survey of the Bad Creek reservoir site and transmission line right-of-way in the spring and fall, respectively, of 1973. This survey was conducted by Dr. Leland Rodgers and J.E. Green in the spring, and Dr. Rodgers in the fall. They found four herbaceous parts that they characterized as rare or rare in the geographical area. The four are Ginseng (Panax quinquefolium), (Figure 2-23), Fraser's lysimachia (Lysimachia fraseri), American climbing fern (Lygodium palmatum), and wintergreen (Gaultheria procumbens). Ginseng has become rare in most parts of the range as a result of the gathering of its highly prized roots for export to China for medicinal purposes.
